\begin{abstract}
Formal verification suffers from the cost of specification: to establish high-level facts, contracts have to be written for supporting functions, many of them mechanical and low-level. 
Specification inference derives such contracts from the program. 
We present a hybrid of agentic and mechanical inference for Move, a smart contract language similar to Rust, integrated with the Move Prover.
An agent controls inference and verification through a tool that, besides calling the Move Prover, derives specifications from code by weakest-precondition analysis.
With this tool, and with loop invariants it proposes itself, the agent derives complete specifications for non-trivial problems.
We evaluate the approach on 26 verification targets, 24 of them extracted from public Move code of the Aptos framework that has no specification, under a frontier model, Sol~5.6, and a mid-tier model of the same family, Terra~5.6. Without \WP, the agent completes 99\% of its cells under the frontier model and 93\% under the mid-tier model. \WP leaves completeness unchanged and lowers the cost by 11--21\%; on targets without loops, the hybrid tactics cost 36--60\% of the agent alone. The mid-tier model costs 53--59\% of the frontier model and falls behind it mainly on one target that needs a permutation argument.

	\keywords{Specification inference \and Weakest precondition \and Reference elimination \and LLM agents \and Move Prover}
\end{abstract}

\subsubsection*{Data Availability Statement.}
The corpus is published with the inference plugin at~\Anon{\cite{MoveFlow}}{\cite{MoveFlowAnon}}: the package extracted from a pinned commit of the Aptos repository, the reference specifications, and both mutant sets.
The round archives behind every table and figure --- per-cell costs, token counters, wall times, and mutant outcomes --- and the scripts that produce them from the archives are published there as well; \Anon{\cite{SpecInferenceCorpus}}{\cite{MoveFlowAnon}} explains how to verify the corpus, re-score a round, and rerun the experiment.

Tables~\ref{tab:sol} and~\ref{tab:terra} give, for each target and arm, the mean cost per cell over the four replicates, mean input/output tokens in thousands (I/O k), the hybrid mean cost as a percentage of agent-only (vs. agent), and whether the specification killed every withheld mutant in all four replicates (\Checkmark) or a mutant survived (\XSolidBrush, subscripted with the count where more than one replicate failed); $\circ$ marks an unmeasured cell.
Input counts include cached tokens.
The targets above the middle rule have no loop that needs an invariant.
